newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: YACHTING-MAORI ACTIVIST TAKES SLEDGEHAMMER TO AMERICA'S CUP.
newsitem.headline: YACHTING-MAORI ACTIVIST TAKES SLEDGEHAMMER TO AMERICA'S CUP.

text.p: A man shouting Maori slogans attacked yachting's America's Cup with a sledgehammer on Friday and inflicted serious damage on the historic trophy, New Zealand police said.
Police spokeswoman Joanne Gibbs said a Maori man walked into the room where the cup was on display at the Royal New Zealand Yacht Squadron in Auckland around noon.
She said the man, dressed in a suit, took a sledgehammer from a bag and rained blows on the glass cabinet containing the trophy, known as the Auld Mug.
"He then took off his suit to indicate that he had some sort of protest T-shirt underneath, shouted a few things and he was then held on to by people who were there," Gibbs said.
"I believe it was some sort of Maori activist protest," she told Reuters. A leaflet left at the scene claimed the act was the work of a Maori liberation organisation.

Police have yet to name the man, but described him as a 27-year-old student from Manurewa, near Auckland. He will appear in the Auckland District Court on Saturday on one charge of criminal damage. Police are considering other charges.
Police said the incident occurred around noon when the man walked into the building at Westhaven Marina and went into the room where the cup was kept in a glass display cabinet.
"A short handled sledgehammer was then allegedly used to smash the cabinet and hit the cup numerous times, leaving it badly damaged," Senior Sergeant Gary Allcock said.
Squadron events manger Harold Evans, who witnessed the incident, said his first reaction was to apprehend the man.
"But seeing someone obviously enraged with a hammer in his hand... I didn't think it was a smart move," he said.
Maoris, the original Polynesian settlers of New Zealand, now make up about 13 percent of the population. A small group of activists has led sporadic campaigns for Maori sovereignty.
The solid silver cup, which is insured for an undisclosed sum, arrived in New Zealand to ticker tape parades in 1995 after Team New Zealand beat Denis Conner's Stars and Stripes in San Diego.
No estimate of the damage was immediately available, but the cup was insured for US$2 million when it was held by the San Diego Yacht Club.
Winning the trophy, which in 144 years was wrested from the United States only once before, prompted an outpouring of national pride.
Team New Zealand leader Sir Peter Blake, who was knighted for his efforts in securing the cup, said he was shocked by Friday's attack on the trophy.
"I'm saddened that someone would want to do this," he said.
New York Yacht Club Vice Commodore George Isdale condemned the attack and said the values represented by the trophy would remain untarnished.
"We are sure the people of New Zealand are as distressed as we are about this senseless act of violence," he said in a written statement.
